video_title: Why the Oil Supply Crunch Isn't Over Yet | Rory Johnston
gist: Rory Johnson (Commodity Context) argues the late-2026 oil selloff reflects lagged October Hormuz flows and washed-out positioning, while markets are complacent about a ~25% daily risk of losing 5 mb/d of Hormuz supply with inventories below five-year lows. Structurally the market is in an OPEC-driven glut that would push Brent toward $40 absent war, but diesel/refining tightness, a jurisdictional premium for safe assets, and China's hidden stock draws (and likely restocking) reshape the picture.

insights.claim: Crude fell roughly 18% on Nymex and 21% on Brent over the month to late November 2026 after peaking near $115-118 Brent just before the US midterm elections.
insights.speaker: host (Maggie Lake)
insights.so_what: Sizes the unwind of the pre-midterm war premium; context for mean-reversion trades.

insights.claim: Rory Johnson attributes the pre-midterm spike to market expectations that Trump would escalate the war with Iran before the elections; when that did not happen the premium unwound and momentum selling followed.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Event-driven escalation premia can deflate fast once the catalyst date passes.

insights.claim: Net speculative positioning in crude (CFTC and ICE Commitments of Traders) has fallen to its lowest level since the rollout after the June-July Memorandum of Understanding, leaving the market oversold and primed for a short-term bounce.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Washed-out positioning argues against chasing shorts; watch COT data for a squeeze setup.
insights.quote: right now, just based on positioning, we are oversold. And I think we'll see some kind of surge here

insights.claim: October 2026 saw the largest volume of oil transiting the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, even as Iranian attacks on shipping increased.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Explains the bearish physical turn of November despite headline risk.

insights.claim: Brent hit almost $120 at end-October while fundamentals were probably in the first global monthly surplus since the war started, which Johnson explains as a roughly month-and-a-half lag between Hormuz flows and their arrival in physical markets.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Price and fundamentals can be out of phase by ~6 weeks; trade the lagged arrival of barrels, not the transit headline.

insights.claim: Johnson's call: if the recent decline in Hormuz transits persists through end-November and into December, physical oil markets will strengthen fundamentally as those supply shortfalls land.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Sets up a December physical tightening; bullish for prompt spreads if transit data stays weak.

insights.claim: The consensus narrative that Middle East supply has 'fully recovered from the Hormuz shock' is stale, based on headlines three to four weeks old, according to Johnson.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the bearish consensus; supports leaning long into the oversold tape.

themes.theme: Reading a high-frequency, distrusted oil market

insights.claim: In a market where every data point has counter-data and nobody trusts anything, Johnson says the only trustworthy signals are realized physical market indicators such as term structure and North Sea front-line spreads.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Prioritize physical spreads and curve shape over contested flow/tanker data.
insights.quote: the only thing people can really trust are these physical realized market signals

insights.claim: Physical market indicators are short-sighted: a surplus visible at a given moment reflects prior flows, so they can mislead on the forward trajectory.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Combine physical signals with forward flow estimates; don't extrapolate a single month's surplus.

insights.claim: Normal oil markets swing by about 1-2% of global balances (a 1 mb/d deficit to 2 mb/d surplus) and evolve slowly, whereas Hormuz transits are now changing by about 4.5 million barrels per day month to month, something not seen outside early COVID.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Monthly data with a two-month lag is obsolete; volatility regime justifies higher implied vols and faster rebalancing.
insights.quote: Every month we see changes of 4.5 million barrels per day. We've never seen anything like this

insights.claim: Tanker-tracking data for Hormuz popular on X is less accurate than markets are used to because shipping behavior keeps changing with the threat environment, creating false signals.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Discount social-media tanker counts; noisy data amplifies sentiment swings.

insights.claim: Johnson's key monitoring rule: sustained contango on both the physical Brent curve and the futures curve for more than a month or two would signal the crisis is genuinely easing; anything shorter is noise.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: A concrete trigger for flipping from tight-market to surplus positioning.
insights.quote: if we see contango on the physical curve and then contango on the futures curve for, say, more than a month or two, that's a sign that things are really starting to ease up

insights.claim: In early November the front of the physical Brent curve and the CFD curve flipped into contango (spot North Sea Brent below two-month forward) even while futures stayed inverted, the most bearish signal Johnson saw; over the past three weeks it has reverted to backwardation, mirroring the June-July 'mini-glut'.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Transient contango episodes reflect clustered tanker arrivals, not a durable glut; fade them unless sustained.

themes.theme: Complacency vs. tail risk in Hormuz supply

insights.claim: Johnson estimates current Hormuz flows at just over 10 million barrels per day versus about 20 million before the war.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Half of pre-war flow remains offline; any further loss hits a thin buffer.

insights.claim: September 2026 showed about a 1 mb/d global deficit, but against a no-war baseline of a 3 mb/d surplus the market is effectively 4 mb/d short of where it would have been.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Judge balances relative to the counterfactual, not to zero; a 'small' deficit is a large shock.
insights.quote: the normal scenario without the war would be 3 million barrels a day of surplus. So we're still 4 million barrels a day short

insights.claim: Global total oil inventories are well below five-year lows after hundreds of millions of barrels were drawn during the war, with commercial and strategic stocks even lower.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Low stocks mean surpluses first refill tanks rather than crush prices; supports a price floor.

insights.claim: Johnson sees roughly a 25% risk that on any given day the market could lose 5 million barrels per day of Hormuz supply via Iranian escalation or a US strike, which he calls unprecedented and underpriced.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Fat right tail argues for cheap upside optionality (calls) in crude.
insights.quote: the fact that we have a 25% risk that on any given day we could lose 5 million barrels of global oil supply per day, we've never lived in an oil market like this

insights.claim: A Libyan pipeline outage costing 350,000 barrels per day, which would have dominated markets for weeks in 2019, is now treated as a rounding error, illustrating how risk perception has shifted.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Mid-sized outages elsewhere are being ignored; cumulative small disruptions may be underpriced.

insights.claim: Johnson views the oil market as structurally bearish if the Iran war ends, but sees no end point in sight, so the current price complacency is unjustified.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Base case bearish only conditional on a peace that isn't visible; position for persistence of risk.
insights.quote: Structurally, this is a bear market if it ever ends. But there doesn't seem to be any end point in sight.

themes.theme: OPEC policy and the structural glut

insights.claim: Johnson's pre-war view was so bearish he expected Brent could be around $40 per barrel at this point in 2026 absent the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Reveals how large the underlying glut is once the war premium is removed.
insights.quote: I thought that at this time of year, in a world where there was no war with Iran, Brent might be worth $40 a barrel

insights.claim: The structural surplus is largely OPEC's making: from October 2022 to early 2024 OPEC+ cut about 6 mb/d (two-thirds of the COVID cut) while prices were above $90, including Saudi Arabia's 'lollipop' unilateral cut in mid-2023, which suppressed demand growth and subsidized US shale growth.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Defending high prices with spare capacity builds a glut that eventually must be released.

insights.claim: Johnson compares OPEC's 2022-2024 cuts to Saudi Arabia's pre-1986 strategy, when North Sea growth let British output exceed Saudi production until the kingdom opened the taps, producing a lost decade for oil in the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Historical analog for a price-war unwind of hoarded spare capacity.

insights.claim: OPEC began rapidly unwinding its cuts in early 2025, putting the market on a glut trajectory designed to force out higher-cost supply, chiefly US shale.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: OPEC market-share strategy targets short-cycle shale; bearish for shale producers when war risk fades.

insights.claim: Long-cycle supply growth from Canada, Guyana, Brazil and Argentina (5-10 year deepwater/oil sands cycles) won't respond to short price drops, leaving US shale as the swing producer that must be rationalized.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Price downside concentrates on shale activity; long-cycle producers keep growing regardless.

insights.claim: Dallas Fed cost curves put the average new-well breakeven in the Permian Basin around $60 per barrel; Johnson saw $40 not as a long-run price but as the level needed to make US shale contract and rebalance the market.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Sub-$60 sustained prices would cut Permian drilling; $40 is a temporary clearing price, not equilibrium.
insights.quote: $40 is not a long-term sustainable price for oil. That was the price that we needed to rationalize enough U.S. supply

insights.claim: Because triple-digit war prices let US shale keep growing instead of contracting, the structural glut has worsened; absent the war, the 2027 surplus should be larger than what was expected for 2026 given another year of OPEC+ growth and weak demand.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: A peace deal in 2027 could trigger a sharper price collapse than consensus expects.

insights.claim: Johnson expects no flood of surplus as long as Middle East supply risk persists, so his base outcome for 2027 hinges entirely on the course of the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Treat 2027 oil as a binary on war resolution; size positions accordingly.

insights.claim: Oil production and reserves located away from the Hormuz conflict zone, such as in the US and Canada, now carry higher implicit option value, a jurisdictional premium for equities holding such assets.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Favor North American producers' reserve valuations over Gulf-exposed assets.
insights.quote: if you have oil production that's not in an area where there are no missiles flying, it's more valuable today

insights.claim: Western refineries once seen as stranded legacy assets have become far more valuable because drones and asymmetric threats make refineries in the Persian Gulf and Russia easy, high-value targets.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Long safe-jurisdiction refiners; refining capacity scarcity is structural.

insights.claim: Russia, the world's third-largest refining center, has had up to half its refining capacity offline at points this year, a Hormuz-scale shock to refining.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Explains outsized product cracks versus crude.

insights.claim: While crude peaked near $120, diesel reached almost $230 per barrel in New York Harbor; diesel cracks went from about $20 pre-COVID (about $30 pre-crisis) to $120 at the September peak and are now about $65, still roughly three times normal.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Diesel tightness persists after crude eases; middle distillate cracks remain the cleaner bullish trade.

insights.claim: EV adoption mainly displaces gasoline, so refiners must recover margins from diesel, while the growth of light US shale crude yields more gasoline and less diesel; both trends structurally push diesel cracks higher.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Structural case for elevated diesel spreads and refiners with high distillate yields.

insights.claim: Farm-state voters were hit hard by diesel prices ahead of the midterms, with agricultural districts telling Johnson that falling gasoline prices did not offset diesel pain affecting all transport and farm equipment.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Diesel is a political pressure point that could drive policy intervention.

insights.claim: AI-driven energy demand is mostly a natural gas story (peaker plants, local turbines), and has reversed the long trend of flat aggregate energy demand; the debate is now about the degree of growth, not direction.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Supports gas-fired power demand regardless of AI equity volatility.

themes.theme: China's hidden stock draw and oil demand

insights.claim: China was the biggest surprise of 2026: it cut crude imports by about 5.5 mb/d, almost half of its total, between February and June-July, which is why Johnson's March call for possible $200 oil missed.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: China acted as a de facto swing buyer; its import behavior now caps and floors prices.
insights.quote: China was the biggest surprise this year

insights.claim: China cut refining by almost 3 mb/d, the steepest in its history, yet trucking activity rose 3.5% year on year while apparent diesel demand fell 20%, implying large unreported draws of underground crude reserves and product (especially diesel) stocks rather than true demand destruction.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Chinese 'demand destruction' was largely inventory draw, so it will be reversed by restocking.

insights.claim: China never acknowledged SPR releases; crude stock estimates rely on satellite readings of floating-roof tanks, which cannot see underground strategic storage or most product storage, making China an inventory black box.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Treat Chinese inventory estimates with wide error bars; flows can swing without warning.

insights.claim: Johnson estimates actual Chinese demand loss at around 1 mb/d, not 5 mb/d-plus, and calls claims that the episode proved the end of the oil era misleading.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Pushes back on peak-oil-demand narratives built on 2026 Chinese import data.

insights.claim: China's EV-driven gasoline displacement has accelerated from about 100-200 kb/d two to three years ago to 500-600 kb/d this year, making Chinese oil demand stagnant at best and possibly negative going forward.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Loss of the historic engine of half of global demand growth is a structural bearish factor.

insights.claim: Johnson's theories for why China drew stocks: protecting domestic price caps, shielding its Asian and European export markets from a Hormuz-driven recession, and possibly stress-testing an energy-security blanket for a Malacca Strait blockade in a Taiwan scenario.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: China demonstrated geopolitical leverage over oil prices larger than the IEA's 400 million barrel coordinated release.

insights.claim: Johnson expects China to restock crude and products if prices fall to $50-60, and with commercial inventories very low globally, a return to surplus would first push the front of the futures curve into contango before a true glut and price crush.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnson
insights.so_what: Chinese restocking creates a soft floor in the $50-60 range; watch curve shape for glut confirmation.
